concepts.definition: Organs and passages that condition and move air, exchange O₂ and CO₂, contribute to pH control, support speech and smell, and defend the airways.
Bulk movement of air into and out of the lungs caused by pressure differences.
Movement of O₂ and CO₂ across respiratory or tissue exchange surfaces by diffusion.
Lung-related ventilation, gas exchange, and blood transport that supply oxygen and eliminate carbon dioxide; the lecture uses this broad three-step sense.
Exchange of O₂ and CO₂ between systemic capillary blood and body tissues; distinct from cellular ATP production.
Cellular metabolic reactions that capture energy, typically using O₂ in aerobic respiration to produce ATP.
Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx in the course's anatomical division.
Larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and lungs in the course's anatomical division.
Airways that transport, filter, warm, and humidify air but do not directly perform alveolar gas exchange.
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli where gas exchange can occur.
The sense of smell, supported by specialized receptors in the nasal cavity.
Control of blood pH; ventilation changes CO₂ removal and therefore influences the bicarbonate buffer system.
Warming, humidifying, and filtering inspired air before it reaches vulnerable exchange surfaces.
Openings of the external nose through which air enters and leaves.
Entrance region of the nasal cavity containing coarse hairs and skin-like lining.
Coarse hairs in the nasal vestibule that trap larger airborne particles.
Air-filled passages behind the external nose that filter, warm, humidify, and convey inspired air.
Midline partition separating the right and left nasal cavities.
Curved projections of the lateral nasal wall that increase surface area and cause air turbulence.
Highest of the three principal nasal conchae, projecting into the upper nasal cavity.
Concha between the superior and inferior conchae, part of the ethmoid bone.
Lowest principal concha, a separate facial bone along the lateral nasal wall.
Air passage beneath a concha within the nasal cavity.
Paired posterior openings connecting the nasal cavity to the nasopharynx.
Air-filled spaces in skull bones that communicate with the nasal cavity.
Bony anterior roof of the mouth separating oral and nasal cavities.
Muscular posterior continuation of the palate that elevates to close the nasopharynx during swallowing.
Midline projection of the soft palate that contributes to closure and sound articulation.
Muscular common passageway for air and, in some portions, swallowed material.
Upper pharyngeal subdivision behind the nasal cavity, used chiefly for air passage.
Middle pharyngeal subdivision posterior to the oral cavity that conveys air and swallowed material.
Lower pharyngeal subdivision that leads anteriorly toward the larynx and posteriorly to the esophagus.
Tube connecting the nasopharynx to the middle ear to help equalize pressure.
Mucous membrane covering much of the conducting airway, comprising respiratory epithelium and underlying connective tissue.
Common ciliated, mucus-producing lining of much of the conducting respiratory tract.
Epithelium whose nuclei lie at different heights, with cilia and often goblet cells, typical of many conducting airways.
Loose connective tissue directly beneath the airway epithelium that supports vessels, nerves, and immune cells.
Epithelial cell that secretes protective mucus to trap particles and pathogens.
Hydrated secretion that traps particles and helps protect and moisten airway surfaces.
Motile hairlike cell-surface projections that drive mucus toward the pharynx in much of the conducting tract.
Ciliary transport of mucus and trapped material upward toward the pharynx for swallowing or expulsion.
Multiple cell layers that resist abrasion in regions such as the oro- and laryngopharynx.
Single layer of cube-shaped cells often found lining smaller bronchioles.
Thin, flattened single-cell layer facilitating gas diffusion in alveolar walls.
Secretory bronchiolar epithelial cell contributing to airway protection and local epithelial maintenance.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Cartilaginous airway organ between pharynx and trachea that protects the airway and enables phonation.
Leaf-shaped elastic cartilage that helps divert swallowed material away from the laryngeal inlet.
Large unpaired laryngeal cartilage forming much of the anterior and lateral laryngeal wall.
Anterior projection of the thyroid cartilage, commonly called the Adam's apple.
Unpaired ring-shaped laryngeal cartilage immediately above the first tracheal ring.
One of a paired set of laryngeal cartilages that moves the vocal folds to open, close, or adjust the glottis.
Small paired cartilage perched on the apex of an arytenoid cartilage.
Small paired cartilage within the aryepiglottic folds that helps support the laryngeal inlet.
Opening between the true vocal folds, together with associated vocal-fold structures in broader usage.
True vocal cords containing ligaments and muscles that vibrate during phonation.
Superior folds above the true vocal folds that help protect the airway.
Production of voiced sound by vibration of the true vocal folds.
Shaping of voiced or unvoiced sound into recognizable speech using tongue, lips, palate, and other structures.
Perceived frequency of vocal-fold vibration, influenced by fold length, mass, and tension.
Muscles that alter vocal-fold position, tension, and glottic opening.
Muscles that move or stabilize the larynx as a whole, including during swallowing.
Suspended neck bone providing attachment for muscles of tongue, pharynx, and larynx.
Defensive sequence of inhalation, glottic closure, pressure buildup, then explosive glottic opening to expel irritants.
Cartilage-supported conducting airway between larynx and primary bronchi.
C-shaped hyaline cartilage ring that resists airway collapse while leaving posterior flexibility.
Posterior smooth-muscle band bridging tracheal cartilage ends and changing airway diameter.
Elastic elements in the tracheal wall that permit lengthening and elastic recoil.
Internal ridge where the trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi.
Main bronchus carrying air from the trachea into one lung.
Lobar bronchus supplying one lung lobe.
Segmental bronchus supplying a bronchopulmonary segment.
Branching airway network from main bronchi through bronchioles toward gas-exchange surfaces.
Usually wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left; aspirated objects more often enter it.
Small airways without cartilage, whose smooth muscle strongly influences airflow resistance.
Final purely conducting bronchiole before respiratory bronchioles begin.
First bronchiolar segment with scattered alveoli and capacity for gas exchange.
Widening of bronchioles, reducing airflow resistance; often promoted by sympathetic β₂-adrenergic signaling.
Narrowing of bronchioles due to smooth-muscle contraction, increasing airflow resistance.
Vagal cholinergic activity commonly promotes bronchoconstriction and secretion in conducting airways.
Lung with superior, middle, and inferior lobes separated by horizontal and oblique fissures.
Lung with superior and inferior lobes, an oblique fissure, and a cardiac notch.
Upper lobe of either lung.
Lobe found only in the right lung, between horizontal and oblique fissures.
Lower lobe of each lung, resting partly above the diaphragm.
Right-lung groove separating superior and middle lobes.
Fissure dividing the inferior lobe from upper lobe territory, present in both lungs.
Anterior indentation of the left lung that accommodates the heart.
Superior pointed region of a lung projecting toward the root of the neck.
Broad inferior surface that sits against the diaphragm.
Medial entry and exit region for bronchi, vessels, lymphatics, and nerves.
Central thoracic compartment containing heart, major vessels, trachea, esophagus, and other structures.
Double-layered serous membrane surrounding each lung and lining the thoracic wall.
Serous membrane directly covering the outer surface of a lung.
Serous membrane lining the thoracic cavity wall, diaphragm, and mediastinal boundaries.
Thin potential space between visceral and parietal pleura containing lubricating fluid.
Pressure within the pleural space, normally below atmospheric pressure during quiet breathing.
Functionally discrete lung region ventilated by a segmental bronchus.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Tiny thin-walled pulmonary air space where gases exchange with surrounding capillary blood.
Cluster of alveoli opening into a common chamber.
Small distal airway lined by openings of alveoli, connecting respiratory bronchioles to sacs.
Thin-walled pulmonary blood vessel closely apposed to alveolar surfaces.
Extremely thin squamous alveolar epithelial cell forming most of the gas-exchange surface.
Alveolar epithelial cell that secretes surfactant and helps replenish alveolar lining cells.
Phagocytic immune cell that removes inhaled debris and microorganisms within alveoli.
Lipid-protein mixture that reduces surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface and stabilizes alveoli.
Cohesive force along a liquid surface that tends to reduce its area; in alveoli it favors collapse without surfactant.
Extremely thin air-to-blood diffusion barrier formed mainly by type I alveolar epithelium, basement membrane, and capillary endothelium.
Closely associated basal laminae of alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium that keep diffusion distance small.
Single endothelial cell layer lining the capillary side of the respiratory membrane.
Passive tendency of stretched lung tissue to return toward smaller volume after inhalation.
Volume of fresh air reaching gas-exchanging alveoli each minute, excluding dead-space ventilation.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: For a fixed quantity of gas at constant temperature, pressure varies inversely with volume (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂).
Pressure exerted by surrounding air; standard sea-level value is about 760 mmHg.
Pressure inside alveoli, which falls slightly below atmosphere in inspiration and rises above it in expiration.
Difference in pressure that drives bulk air movement from higher toward lower pressure.
Inhalation as thoracic expansion lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure.
Exhalation as lung recoil or expiratory muscle activity raises alveolar pressure above atmosphere.
Dome-shaped skeletal muscle and chief inspiratory muscle; its contraction flattens and expands thoracic volume.
Muscles between ribs that elevate the rib cage and assist inspiration.
Intercostal muscles whose interosseous portions are recruited during forceful expiration; their actions vary by portion.
Additional neck and chest muscles recruited when ventilatory demand or respiratory effort rises.
Resting ventilation with active inspiration and mostly passive expiration.
Ventilation involving additional inspiratory and active expiratory muscle effort during high demand.
Breathing pattern emphasizing rib-cage movements.
Breathing pattern emphasizing contraction and descent of the diaphragm.
Passive tendency of lungs to decrease volume after inspiration; major driver of relaxed expiration.
Opposition to airflow, strongly influenced by airway radius, especially in bronchioles.
Air inhaled or exhaled during one ordinary resting breath.
Additional volume inhalable after a normal inspiration.
Additional air exhalable after an ordinary expiration.
Air left in lungs after the strongest possible expiration.
Greatest amount of air that can be expelled after a maximal inhalation; TV + IRV + ERV.
Maximum volume contained in lungs after full inspiration; VC + RV.
Largest amount inhalable after normal expiration; TV + IRV.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Volume remaining after an ordinary passive expiration; ERV + RV.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Measurement of inhaled/exhaled volumes and flows; ordinary spirometry cannot directly measure residual volume.
Ventilated volume that does not participate in gas exchange during a given breath.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Pressure contributed by one gas in a gas mixture, reflecting its fraction of total gas pressure.
Partial pressure of oxygen, a key determinant of oxygen diffusion and hemoglobin loading.
Partial pressure of carbon dioxide, influencing diffusion and acid–base regulation.
At a fixed temperature, the dissolved concentration of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure and solubility.
Extent to which a gas dissolves in a liquid under given conditions; CO₂ is more soluble in plasma than O₂.
Net passive movement down a concentration or partial-pressure gradient.
Diffusion of O₂ from alveolar gas into pulmonary blood and CO₂ in the reverse direction.
Diffusion of O₂ from systemic blood into tissues and CO₂ from tissues into blood.
Thickness of the barrier gases must cross; thickening reduces exchange efficiency.
Membrane area available for diffusion; loss of alveolar surface reduces capacity for exchange.
Iron-containing red-cell protein that binds and transports most oxygen in blood.
Hemoglobin carrying bound oxygen.
Hemoglobin not carrying oxygen at a given binding site.
Sigmoid relation between blood PO₂ and percentage of hemoglobin binding sites carrying oxygen.
Percentage of available hemoglobin O₂-binding sites occupied by oxygen.
Binding of one O₂ molecule increases hemoglobin's affinity for additional O₂ molecules.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Reduced hemoglobin affinity for oxygen when CO₂ or H⁺ increases, favoring O₂ unloading in active tissues.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Association of O₂ with hemoglobin where PO₂ is high, especially in pulmonary capillaries.
Release of bound O₂ from hemoglobin where tissue PO₂ is lower and local conditions favor dissociation.
Strength with which hemoglobin binds oxygen, influenced by pH, CO₂, temperature, and other factors.
Small fraction of blood O₂ physically dissolved in plasma, which contributes directly to PO₂.
Gas generated during metabolism, removed by ventilation and carried in blood in several forms.
Enzyme, abundant in red blood cells, that speeds conversion between CO₂ + H₂O and carbonic acid-related species.
Short-lived acid intermediate (H₂CO₃) in the reversible CO₂/bicarbonate reaction.
HCO₃⁻ ion, the chief form in which most CO₂-derived carbon travels in blood.
Exchange of bicarbonate out of RBCs for chloride into RBCs at tissues, reversed in lungs to support CO₂ exchange.
Hemoglobin with CO₂ chemically bound to its globin portion, not to the iron of heme.
Reversible CO₂/H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ system that helps regulate blood hydrogen-ion concentration.
Fall in blood pH associated with CO₂ retention caused by inadequate ventilation.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Rise in blood pH associated with excessive CO₂ loss during excessive ventilation.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Elevated arterial PCO₂.
Decreased arterial PCO₂.
Brainstem region containing networks essential for generating and modulating respiratory rhythm.
Brainstem structure that modulates breathing pattern through pontine respiratory networks.
Medullary group involved in integrating sensory inputs and influencing inspiratory output.
Medullary network including inspiratory and expiratory neurons recruited according to breathing needs.
Medullary neuronal network crucial to respiratory rhythm generation; modern detail beyond older lecture-center labels.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Historical pontine label for networks that can facilitate prolonged inspiration.
Historical pontine label for networks that help terminate or shape inspiration.
Chemosensitive brainstem neurons primarily responding to CO₂-driven changes in brain extracellular-fluid pH.
Chemosensory structures in carotid and aortic bodies responsive to low arterial PO₂ and also CO₂/pH.
Peripheral chemoreceptor organ near the carotid bifurcation particularly sensitive to arterial oxygen decreases.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Chemoreceptor tissue associated with the aortic arch sensing arterial blood gases.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Motor nerve from cervical spinal levels C3–C5 supplying the diaphragm.
concepts.scopeNote: Supplemental scientific context; not necessarily an explicit lecture term.

concepts.definition: Recurring neural pattern generating inspiration and expiration.
Sensory receptor responding to pulmonary inflation; can help modulate inspiratory activity.
Airway sensory ending that triggers protective reflexes such as cough upon stimulation.
Feedback adjustment of breathing triggered by changes in blood gases or pH.
Insufficient oxygen availability in body tissues.
Extreme or near-complete lack of usable oxygen in tissues.
Inflammation of the larynx, often altering vocal fold vibration and voice quality.
Inflammation of the epiglottis that can dangerously obstruct the upper airway.
Infection/inflammation involving lung tissue and alveoli, often impairing gas exchange through exudate or fluid.
Inherited CFTR-related disease causing dehydrated, thick airway mucus and impaired clearance with recurrent infection risk.
Chronic airway disease with variable airflow limitation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and often inflammation.
